parts.note: a prover is one who proves or demonstrates something
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A protester marches out ahead of a church dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a verb or a tool, but it is a noun meaning an old saying. 'before' simply puts PROVER ahead of B.
explanation.definitionFit: An old saw is a traditional saying or maxim.

explanation.walkthrough: French polish is a glossy shellac finish for furniture, so 'French' qualifies the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue of Poland; also a shine or wood finish, of which French polish is a variety.

parts.note: odd men are eccentric people

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the word accept is used

explanation.surface: Weird people take what remains at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accept' looks like a container signal but here merely supplies its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: A leftover scrap or remnant is what remains after the rest is used.

indicators.note: the two words share letters where they meet, so the common run is written once

parts.note: Easter is the Christian spring festival
sterner means stricter

explanation.surface: An Eastern celebration grows harsher as it coincides with another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when overlapping' runs EASTER into STERNER, sharing the STER they have in common: EA + STERNER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the East is an Oriental in the old sense of the word.

parts.note: broad is dated American slang for a woman
minded means took heed of or noted

explanation.surface: A US woman is a well-known member of a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' is capitalised to suggest the party; it means tolerant.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerant of others' views, open and unprejudiced.

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-husband
a mouth is the organ one speaks with; slangily a talker

explanation.surface: A one-time public speaker has retired to the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is elliptical: the answer is a place in Devon, the English county in the south-west. EXMOUTH is a seaside town there at the mouth of the river Exe.
explanation.definitionFit: The seaside town sits on the south coast of that English county, so 'in Devon' locates it.

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense alludes to 'an eye for an eye', tit-for-tat punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: To watch something; also the biblical law of an eye for an eye, matching revenge to injury.

parts.note: score means write music, so this is a tempo instruction in Italian telling players to go quickly

explanation.surface: A tip for racking up points quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' suggests winning points; it is a musical score, and the answer is an Italian marking meaning with movement, i.e. quicker.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian musical direction meaning animated, played with movement and speed.

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the prefix ought to make the word mean not loose, though it actually means loosen.
explanation.definitionFit: To set free or untie; read literally as 'not loose', it seems to mean taut.

parts.note: Hun is a derogatory old term for a German
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A German wig is meant for a woman called Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt; 'hair-piece' suggests a wig but means a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess Diana presided over the chase, so she is the archetypal female hunter.

clue.text: Something attractive in oldest one switching first couple

indicators.note: the opening pair of letters of the phrase oldest one change places with each other

explanation.surface: The most aged item has a magnetic charm, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first two letters of OLDESTONE gives LODESTONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturally magnetised rock draws iron towards it, so it is literally attractive.

indicators.note: cut short, so the final letter of the goodbye is dropped

parts.note: so long is an informal goodbye

explanation.surface: A sage keeps his goodbyes short.
explanation.walkthrough: SOLON was the lawgiver of ancient Athens, his name now used for any wise legislator; 'brief' trims SO LONG to SOLON.
explanation.definitionFit: Solon was an Athenian statesman famed for wisdom, and his name stands for any sage lawmaker.

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful: a swede (the turnip-like root, called rutabaga in America) is growth under the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swede is a native of Sweden; the root vegetable called a swede also grows beneath the soil, a whimsical sense of 'undergrowth'.

clue.text: Remove king or queen, say? Shame!

explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the top cards (ace, king, queen, jack, ten) are called honours, hence the question mark on the whimsical first reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Court cards like king and queen are honours in bridge, so stripping one is jocularly to remove an honour; disgrace is the plain sense.

clue.text: Keeping apart from Saint George, somehow

indicators.note: in some way or other, so the letters are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: Staying away from England's patron saint by some means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' shuffles all the letters of SAINT GEORGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Separation of groups, the act of setting them apart from each other.

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase: orders that make people stand would end their sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Permanent rules governing how a parliament conducts business; whimsically, commands to rise ending a session in seats.

clue.text: Note producer's mixture of red and orange

indicators.note: the letters of the two colour words are mixed together into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A painter's blend of two colours makes a third.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixture of' rearranges REDORANGE; 'and' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard instrument sounding through vibrating reeds produces musical tones.

explanation.walkthrough: A neat whisky is taken straight; the home straight is part of a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Undiluted, as a spirit served without water; also the level stretch of a racetrack.

clue.text: Wine cask game writer found in English resort

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer
bridge is a card game
H G Wells was the author of The War of the Worlds

explanation.surface: A barrel of wine, a card table and a novelist turn up at a spa town.
explanation.walkthrough: TUNBRIDGE WELLS is a spa town in Kent, south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Tunbridge Wells is a historic spa town in Kent, long a fashionable place to take the waters.

clue.text: Work manually and complete, we hear, what's required

indicators.note: the words are recognised by how they are spoken, not spelt

parts.note: to knead dough is to work it by hand; full means complete

explanation.surface: Handle dough by hand and finish it: that's what is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: KNEAD (silent K) + FULL said together sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The necessary thing, as in 'do the needful', meaning what must be done.

parts.note: a mere is a lake, which in French is lac
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: France's monarch was found wanting, mere figurehead that he was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mere' looks like 'only' or the French 'mère' (mother); it is the English word for a lake, translated into French.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting or short of something, missing what is needed.

indicators.note: the river's letter goes within the other letters

parts.note: even means level

explanation.surface: A river runs through flat land in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the wordplay and also describes the answer, Britain's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest river in Britain, flowing through the south-west into the Bristol Channel.

clue.text: She makes porter cross, as well as artist

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, a kind of ale
X is the shape of a cross
and means as well as
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A woman annoys the hotel doorman and also a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porter' and 'cross' pretend to be a doorman and an adjective meaning angry; they are beer and the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, so any woman bearing it can be called 'she'.

indicators.note: thrown about, so the letters of caber land in a new order

explanation.surface: The thrown pole at the Highland games is pointed.
explanation.walkthrough: Tossing the caber is a Scottish Highland games event, so 'Tossed' fits the surface while signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare word for bitter or acid in taste or temper, as in acerbic.

explanation.walkthrough: Players of snooker and pool chalk the tip of their stick (the cue) to stop it slipping.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving exactly at the right moment; also snooker chalk is rubbed on to the tip of the stick.

clue.text: Blunder, repeating third note in quartet

parts.note: a run of four musical note letters A to G in which the third one is played twice, giving five letters

explanation.surface: A musician makes a slip by playing one note of a quartet twice.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the answer is a musical note name (A to G): four different notes, with the third doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: A social or verbal slip that causes embarrassment, a faux pas.

parts.note: doing means operating or performing
from the saying that time is the great healer

explanation.surface: A surgeon is at work with an eminent doctor in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' looks like part of the medical scene, but is slang for in prison; the answer is the phrase for serving a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inside means being in jail, which is serving a sentence.

clue.text: Forget lines may be out of water

explanation.walkthrough: To dry, in acting jargon, is to forget one's lines on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre slang for an actor blanking on the script; also simply not wet.

parts.note: someone grown up has become tall
a boy is a male child

explanation.surface: Something to furnish a home suitable for both adult and youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: A TALLBOY is a tall chest of drawers, often one set on another.
explanation.definitionFit: A high chest of drawers, a piece of bedroom storage.

clue.text: Figure concealed by Venetian on a gondola

indicators.note: the letters sit tucked away inside the words Venetian on a gondola

explanation.surface: A shape is hidden by a Venetian riding in a gondola.
explanation.definitionFit: A nine-sided polygon is a geometric figure.
